claims.text: Spark plasma sintering can densify single-phase ZrB2 at temperatures below 1700 °C.
SPS below 1700 °C will preserve strong Zr–B and B–B interactions.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have enhanced oxidation durability relative to conventionally processed and other lower-temperature specimens.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have improved resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion relative to conventionally processed and other lower-temperature specimens.
The proposed intervention is to use SPS as the sole processing-route modification for densification below 1700 °C.
Rapid heating and short dwell times under an inert or vacuum atmosphere are the proposed SPS conditions.
SPS will produce a refined, highly dense microstructure with controlled grain growth.
Rapid SPS densification minimizes high-temperature exposure.
Minimized high-temperature exposure reduces grain coarsening.
Minimized high-temperature exposure limits oxidation during processing.
The resulting dense microstructure maintains favorable Zr–B and B–B interactions.
Maintaining the dense microstructure and favorable bonding interactions increases resistance to high-temperature oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion.
SPS-produced ZrB2 will have equivalent or improved intrinsic strength relative to both comparator routes.
Refined microstructure and fewer processing-induced defects are responsible for the predicted improvements in oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering temperatures above 2300 °C.
Traditional lower-temperature routes fail to achieve optimal densification and microstructural integrity.
The hypothesis applies to moderate-to-high-temperature oxidative service and liquid-metal plating-bath service.
SPS is known to produce dense materials at lower temperatures.
The extent to which SPS mitigates liquid plating-metal corrosion is uncertain.
